(CNN) -- At 44-years-old Abhisit Vejjajiva is Thailand's youngest prime minister in more than 60 years. But perhaps more immediately significantly, he is the country's third prime minister in four months after a period of immense upheaval in Thailand. After just two days of taking office, Thai PM Abhisit Vejjajiva talked to CNN's Dan Rivers for Talk Asia. Thailand's recent political turmoil, which included national demonstrations and the forced closures of international airports, dates back to the 2006 coup that overthrew former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra, the former People's Power Party leader. In September, the Constitutional Court forced out his replacement Samak Sundaravej, finding that he had violated the constitution by appearing as a paid guest on a television cooking show. In turn he was replaced by Thaksin's brother-in-law, Somchai Wongsawat, who immediately found himself beset by opposition demonstrations that accused him of leading a proxy government for Thaksin. He too was thrown out by a Constitutional Court ruling. Abhisit was named as the new Prime Minister on December 15, and his biggest challenge will be to steady a country that until recently was known as one of the most region's most stable. A career politician, Abhisit was born in Newcastle in the north east of England to wealthy Thai-Chinese parents and attended Eton, one of the UK's top private schools before studying politics, philosophy and economics at Oxford University. While highly critical of the corruption and cronyism in Thai politics, Abhisit's own route to power has not been as he may have wanted it. As leader of the Democrat Party since 2005, he failed to win either of the elections he contended. He was chosen by the Thai parliament to be Prime Minister during a special session. His selection was contingent on support of factions from the now banned PPP who changed allegiance, many of whom he had previously criticized. Abhisit now leads a coalition government with a small majority consisting of a number of parties and interests, leading political commentators to speculate about the length of his tenure in office, many suggesting more than a year in power would be a success. Countering accusations of inexperience, Abhisit can still boast 17 years of political practice, having become a parliamentarian at the age of 27. As well as being young and cosmopolitan, he has gained a reputation as being above the sleaze and corruption that has dogged many other Thai politicians, while he publicly opposed the bloodless military coup that removed Thaksin from office 2006. However critics have said that his policies are borrowed heavily from Thaksin and that his party's decision to boycott the snap election in 2006 led to the constitutional crisis and coup against Thaksin. Most of Abhisit's support comes from the educated middle classes and gaining support, or at least lessening the divisions between sections of Thai society is something he has been immediately faced with. "He needs to send a clear signal of change that he is a leader who will reach out to all," said Bunranaj Smutharak, a spokesman for Abhisit's Democrat Party. "We are confident the long turmoil over the past two years will be brought to an end by this change in government," he said. "What we set out to do is reunite the country."

A career politician, Abhisit was born in Newcastle in northeastern England to affluent Thai-Chinese parents. He attended Eton, one of the UK’s elite private schools, before earning a degree in Politics, Philosophy, and Economics at Oxford University. 

Though a vocal critic of corruption and cronyism in Thai politics, Abhisit’s path to the premiership was far from ideal. Having led the Democrat Party since 2005, he failed to win either of the general elections he contested. Instead, he was elected Prime Minister by the Thai parliament during a special session. His victory relied heavily on the support of defecting factions from the now-banned PPP—figures he had previously criticized. 

Abhisit now heads a fragile coalition government with a narrow parliamentary majority. This precarious standing has led political commentators to speculate on the longevity of his administration, with many suggesting that surviving even a single year in power would be a major triumph. 

To counter accusations of inexperience, Abhisit points to his 17 years of active parliamentary service, having first won a seat at the age of 27. Alongside his youth and cosmopolitan background, he has cultivated a reputation for remaining untainted by the sleaze and corruption that have long dogged Thai political life; he also publicly opposed the bloodless 2006 coup that removed Thaksin. Nevertheless, critics contend that his platform borrows heavily from Thaksin's policies, and they argue that his party's decision to boycott the 2006 snap election directly precipitated the constitutional crisis and subsequent coup.

With the majority of his support rooted in the educated middle class, Abhisit’s most immediate challenge is to bridge the country's deep socio-political divides and broaden his political appeal.

**Title:** Navigating the Divide: Abhisit Vejjajiva and Thailand’s Fragile Quest for Stability

By late 2008, Thailand was a nation brought to a standstill by years of relentless political warfare. A cycle of massive street protests, military intervention, and judicial activism had torn at the fabric of Thai society, leaving the country deeply polarized. The defining feud between the "Yellow Shirts"—royalist, urban elites who opposed the influence of ousted former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra—and the "Red Shirts"—predominantly rural, working-class supporters of Thaksin—had crippled normal governance.

The turmoil reached a fever pitch in late November 2008, when anti-Thaksin protesters seized Bangkok’s two main international airports, stranding hundreds of thousands of tourists and devastating the national economy. Shortly thereafter, Thailand’s Constitutional Court dissolved the ruling pro-Thaksin People Power Party (PPP) over electoral fraud, forcing Prime Minister Somchai Wongsawat from office. Somchai was the second head of state ousted in just three months, following his predecessor Samak Sundaravej, who had been removed on a judicial technicality.

It was against this chaotic backdrop that Abhisit Vejjajiva, the British-born, Oxford-educated leader of the opposition Democrat Party, emerged as the country's new leader in December 2008. 

Unlike many of his predecessors, Abhisit did not ascend to the prime ministership through a direct victory in a general election. Instead, he secured power through a series of calculated parliamentary realignments. Capitalizing on the political vacuum left by the dissolution of the PPP, Abhisit’s party, with the discrete encouragement of the military and key political power brokers, successfully convinced several minor coalition partners and a major faction of former Thaksin loyalists—led by veteran politician Newin Chidchob—to switch sides. On December 15, 2008, the House of Representatives elected Abhisit as the 27th Prime Minister of Thailand.

Upon taking office, Abhisit faced an unprecedented array of challenges. Externally, the 2008 global financial crisis was threatening Thailand's export-reliant economy. Internally, the country’s democratic institutions were severely eroded, and public trust in the political system had practically evaporated. Abhisit sought to present himself as a stabilizing force—a young, articulate, and reform-minded leader who could restore economic health, mend the rule of law, and project an image of calm professionalism abroad. 

His administration swiftly launched economic stimulus packages to cushion the blow of the global recession and introduced policies aimed at rural development and expanding public education and healthcare. Abhisit also preached national reconciliation, offering a vision of governance rooted in transparency and institutional integrity.

However, the very nature of his rise to power proved to be his greatest political vulnerability. To his supporters, his appointment was a constitutional, parliamentary solution that legitimately resolved a national emergency. To his detractors—most notably the Red Shirts organized under the United Front for Democracy Against Dictatorship (UDD)—his government was viewed as an illegitimate regime, born not of the popular will expressed at the ballot box, but of "backroom deals" brokered by the military and judicial establishments. 

This crisis of legitimacy meant that Abhisit’s quest for stability was uphill from the start. His premiership was ultimately plagued by renewed street demonstrations, climaxing in major violent clashes in Bangkok in April 2009 and spring 2010, which left scores dead and hundreds injured.

Despite these overwhelming obstacles, Abhisit Vejjajiva’s tenure remains a critical chapter in modern Thai political history. His leadership marked a pivotal attempt to steer Thailand away from total institutional collapse and navigate a path toward civil governance amidst unprecedented division. While he succeeded in keeping the state machinery functioning through a period of extreme vulnerability, his term underscored the profound difficulty of uniting a fractured nation where the fundamental rules of power remain fiercely contested.

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a detailed overview of how Abhisit Vejjajiva became Thailand's Prime Minister in 2008 and the political turmoil that preceded his rise.
counterfactuals.output:
The ascent of Abhisit Vejjajiva to the Prime Ministership of Thailand in December 2008 marked a dramatic turning point in modern Thai political history. It was the culmination of three years of intense political polarization, street protests, military interventions, and controversial judicial rulings. 

Abhisit, an Oxford-educated politician and leader of the conservative, establishment-backed Democrat Party, did not assume power through a general election victory. Instead, he took office through parliamentary maneuvers facilitated by judicial rulings that dissolved the ruling party and a crucial realignment of political factions brokered behind the scenes.

Here is a detailed breakdown of the political turmoil that preceded his rise and the mechanics of how Abhisit became Prime Minister.

---

### 1. Context: The Shadow of Thaksin Shinawatra (2001–2007)
To understand 2008, one must understand the deep schism surrounding billionaire populist Thaksin Shinawatra:
* **The Divide:** Thaksin had built an unprecedented voter base among Thailand’s rural and working-class population (mostly in the North and Northeast) through populist policies like universal healthcare and micro-loans. However, he was deeply loathed by the royalist establishment, urban middle class, Southern voters, and the military elite, who accused him of corruption, authoritarianism, and disrespect for the monarchy.
* **The 2006 Coup:** Thaksin was ousted in a military coup in September 2006. The junta drafted a new constitution in 2007 designed to weaken executive power and popular political parties.
* **The 2007 Election:** Despite the military's efforts, when democratic elections were held in December 2007, the **People’s Power Party (PPP)**—a direct proxy for Thaksin—won the most seats. Abhisit’s Democrat Party came in second. The PPP formed a coalition government, proving that Thaksin’s political machine remained dominant.

---

### 2. The 2008 Crisis: Yellow Shirts and Political Paralysis
The pro-Thaksin PPP government took office in early 2008, but it faced immediate, fierce resistance from the **People’s Alliance for Democracy (PAD)**, commonly known as the **"Yellow Shirts."** Representing the royalist establishment and urban elite, the PAD took to the streets to bring down the government.

#### A. The Fall of Samak Sundaravej
* Samak Sundaravej, a veteran right-wing politician, became Prime Minister under the PPP.
* In May 2008, the Yellow Shirts launched continuous street protests. By August, they illegally occupied the **Government House** (the Prime Minister's office complex), paralyzing the administration.
* In September 2008, the Constitutional Court removed Samak from office on a legal technicality: he had accepted a small payment for appearing on a television cooking show while serving as PM, which violated conflict-of-interest laws.

#### B. Somchai Wongsawat and Escalation
* PPP appointed **Somchai Wongsawat**—Thaksin’s brother-in-law—as the new Prime Minister. This further enraged the Yellow Shirts, who saw it as direct rule by Thaksin.
* Somchai was barred from even entering Government House due to the ongoing PAD occupation.
* **The Airport Siege (November 2008):** In late November, the Yellow Shirts escalated their protests to a dangerous high. They stormed and occupied Bangkok’s two main airports, **Suvarnabhumi** and **Don Mueang**. This stranded over 300,000 foreign tourists, cut off international commerce, and caused devastating economic damage to Thailand. The military, led by Army Commander General Anupong Paochinda, refused government orders to clear the airports by force.

---

### 3. The "Judicial Coup" of December 2008
The deadlock ended not through military force, but through the judiciary.

* On **December 2, 2008**, while the airport siege was ongoing, the Constitutional Court issued a landmark ruling.
* Finding the PPP and two of its coalition partners guilty of electoral fraud committed during the 2007 election, the court **dissolved the PPP** and banned Somchai Wongsawat and dozens of executive party members from politics for five years.
* With its top leadership banned and the party legally dissolved, the pro-Thaksin government collapsed, and the Yellow Shirts ended their siege of the airports.

---

### 4. How Abhisit Vejjajiva Reached Power
The dissolution of the PPP created a power vacuum. While the remaining pro-Thaksin MPs quickly regrouped into a new entity called the **Pheu Thai Party**, they no longer held a automatic majority without their banned leaders and former coalition partners.

Abhisit and his top strategist, **Suthep Thaugsuban**, seized the opportunity to form a new government through parliamentary reallocation.

#### A. The Realignment ("Friends of Newin")
* The critical shift came from **Newin Chidchob**, a powerful faction leader from Buriram province within the dissolved PPP.
* Newin controlled a bloc of roughly 30–40 MPs known as the "Friends of Newin." 
* Realizing the military and establishment would never allow another pro-Thaksin government to function smoothly, Newin famously broke ranks with Thaksin, declaring that his loyalty to the country and the monarchy superseded his loyalty to Thaksin.

#### B. The Role of the Military
* Top military commanders, particularly Army Chief **Gen. Anupong Paochinda** and Gen. Prawit Wongsuwan, played a pivotal behind-the-scenes role.
* Reportedly, key negotiations between Abhisit’s Democrats, Newin's faction, and smaller coalition parties took place at an army barracks in Bangkok. The military pressured smaller parties to abandon the pro-Thaksin camp and join the Democrats to restore stability.

#### C. The Parliamentary Vote
* On **December 15, 2008**, the House of Representatives convened to vote for a new Prime Minister.
* Abhisit Vejjajiva defeated the pro-Thaksin candidate, Pracha Promnog, by a vote of **235 to 198**.
* On **December 17, 2008**, Abhisit received royal endorsement, officially becoming Thailand’s 27th Prime Minister at the age of 44.

---

### 5. Aftermath and Legacy of Abhisit's Rise
Abhisit’s ascension brought an end to the Yellow Shirt protests, but it laid the groundwork for the next phase of Thailand's instability:

* **Perception of Illegitimacy:** Supporters of Thaksin viewed Abhisit’s government as a "judicial coup" and an illegitimate administration installed by the military and judges rather than the ballot box.
* **The Rise of the Red Shirts:** Pro-Thaksin forces organized under the banner of the **United Front for Democracy Against Dictatorship (UDD)**, known as the **"Red Shirts."**
* **Subsequent Violence (2009–2010):** The Red Shirts launched massive counter-protests against Abhisit's government. In early 2009, they disrupted the ASEAN summit in Pattaya. In April–May 2010, prolonged Red Shirt occupations of downtown Bangkok ended in a military crackdown ordered by Abhisit's government, resulting in over 90 deaths and thousands of injuries.
* **2011 Election:** When Abhisit finally called an election in July 2011, his Democrat Party was decisively defeated by Thaksin's sister, **Yingluck Shinawatra**, illustrating that the parliamentary shift of 2008 had not changed the fundamental political preferences of the Thai electorate.

### Summary
Abhisit Vejjajiva became Prime Minister through a "backroom realignment" made possible by the legal dissolution of the ruling party, aggressive street pressure by Yellow Shirt protesters, and critical facilitation by the Thai military elite. While it temporarily resolved the late-2008 crisis, it deeply entrenched the Red vs. Yellow divide that defined Thai politics for the next decade.

counterfactuals.output:
**Thailand’s New Leader: Can Abhisit Vejjajiva Heal a Divided Nation?**

**BANGKOK, Thailand (CNN)** — After years of paralyzing street protests, airport blockades, and a revolving door of leadership, Thailand has a new face at the helm. At just 44 years old, Abhisit Vejjajiva has stepped into the political crucible as Thailand’s youngest Prime Minister in over half a century. 

Handsome, fluent in English, and impeccably polished, Abhisit presents a starkly different image from the battle-hardened politicians who preceded him. But behind the photogenic smile lies a daunting task: steering the "Land of Smiles" out of its deepest constitutional and social crisis in modern history. 

This week on *Talk Asia*, CNN sits down with Thailand’s new leader to discuss his meteoric rise, the shadow of his predecessors, and whether a Western-educated elite can truly bridge his country's bitter political divide.

---

### An Oxford Scholar in Bangkok

To his supporters, Abhisit is the epitome of a modern, clean reformer. Born in Newcastle upon Tyne, England, to wealthy Thai medical professors, his pedigree is undeniably elite. He was educated at Eton College—the prestigious British boarding school that produced several British Prime Ministers—before earning a first-class degree in Philosophy, Politics, and Economics (PPE) at Oxford University. 

Returning to Thailand, Abhisit entered politics at just 27, joining the country’s oldest political organization, the Democrat Party. His eloquent speeches, media-savvy style, and technocratic appeal quickly made him a rising star among urban, middle-class voters in Bangkok and the southern provinces.

Yet, this patrician background is a double-edged sword. To his detractors, particularly the rural poor in Thailand's northeast, Abhisit represents the Bangkok-centric establishment—detached from the struggles of the working class and lacking a direct mandate from the people.

---

### The Road Through Chaos: Thaksin, Samak, and Somchai

Abhisit’s path to the premiership was paved by three years of extraordinary political turmoil that paralyzed the nation and severely damaged its tourism-dependent economy.

The crisis stems back to the 2006 military coup that ousted billionaire populist Prime Minister **Thaksin Shinawatra**, whose overwhelming popularity among rural voters threatened the traditional royalist-military establishment. Though exiled, Thaksin’s political shadow remained long and formidable.

When elections returned in late 2007, Thaksin loyalists swept back into power under the People Power Party (PPP), led by the fiery veteran politician **Samak Sundaravej**. Samak’s tenure was brief and chaotic, marked by fierce anti-government protests by the "Yellow Shirts"—the People's Alliance for Democracy (PAD). In a bizarre twist of constitutional law, Samak was forced to resign in September 2008 after the Constitutional Court ruled that accepting payments for hosting a television cooking show breached conflict-of-interest laws.

Samak was succeeded by **Somchai Wongsawat**, who happened to be Thaksin’s brother-in-law. Somchai’s brief premiership saw Thailand pushed to the brink of collapse. Yellow Shirt protesters stormed Bangkok's main international airport, shutting it down for days and stranding hundreds of thousands of tourists. 

The deadlock broke in December 2008, when Thailand’s Constitutional Court dissolved the ruling PPP for electoral fraud and banned its key leaders from politics. 

---

### A Fragile Coalition

It was in the wake of this judicial earthquake that Abhisit seized his moment. Rather than calling a new general election—which Thaksin-aligned parties were widely expected to win again—Abhisit managed to cobble together a parliamentary majority. By persuading key faction leaders from the collapsed ruling party to defect, and securing the quiet backing of the powerful military, Abhisit was voted Prime Minister by Parliament on December 15, 2008.

While his ascension restored temporary calm to the streets and ended the airport blockade, critics argue his government lacks democratic legitimacy. The "Red Shirts"—protesters loyal to Thaksin—view Abhisit’s rise as a "silent coup" engineered by courts, soldiers, and elite power brokers to override the popular vote.

---

### The Challenge Ahead

As Abhisit settles into the Prime Minister’s office, the stakes could not be higher. Thailand is reeling from the dual shocks of internal instability and a global economic downturn. Red Shirt protesters are already gathering, demanding fresh elections, while the royalist elites who helped him to power expect him to purge Thaksin’s lingering influence entirely.

Can a British-educated technocrat convince millions of rural voters that he represents their interests? Can he restore investor confidence and mend a deeply fractured society? 

**Join CNN’s *Talk Asia* as we probe Prime Minister Abhisit Vejjajiva on his controversial ascent, his vision for Thailand’s future, and whether he can keep the peace in one of Southeast Asia's most volatile democracies.**

counterfactuals.output:
**Abhisit Vejjajiva** is a Thai politician who served as the **27th Prime Minister of Thailand from December 2008 to August 2011**. He is also the former leader of the Democrat Party, Thailand’s oldest political party. Known for his articulate speaking style, polished demeanor, and liberal economic views, Abhisit was a central, albeit polarizing, figure during a period of intense political crisis in Thailand.

Below is a summary of his education, political background, and the challenges his administration faced.

---

### 1. Education at Eton and Oxford
Abhisit’s background is deeply rooted in the British elite educational system, which contributed to his cosmopolitan image but later exposed him to criticism from political rivals who portrayed him as an out-of-touch aristocrat.

* **Early Years & Eton College:** Born in Newcastle upon Tyne, England, in 1964 to wealthy, aristocratic Thai parents (both medical professors), Abhisit was sent to England for his secondary education at the prestigious **Eton College**. 
* **Oxford University:** He earned a Bachelor’s degree in **Philosophy, Politics, and Economics (PPE)** with First Class Honors from **St John's College, Oxford**. PPE is widely regarded as the premier degree for British political elites. He later returned to Oxford to complete a Master's degree in Economics. 
* **Academic Return:** Before entering politics full-time, he briefly taught economics at Oxford and later at Chulachomklao Royal Military Academy and Thammasat University in Thailand.

---

### 2. Political Background
Abhisit’s political career began remarkably early, marked by a rapid rise through the Democrat Party:

* **Entry into Politics (1992):** Elected as a Member of Parliament for Bangkok in 1992 at just 27 years old, becoming one of the youngest MPs in Thai history.
* **Party Leadership (2005):** After holding several junior ministerial posts in the 1990s, he was elected leader of the Democrat Party in 2005, positioning himself as a clean, reform-minded alternative to the populist Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra.
* **Rise to Prime Minister (2008):** Abhisit did not become Prime Minister through a general election victory. In late 2008, following months of protests by royalist "Yellow Shirts," the Constitutional Court dissolved the ruling pro-Thaksin party. Abhisit formed a government by piecing together a coalition with smaller parties and defectors from the previous government—a deal widely reported to have been facilitated by the Thai military.
* **Later Career & Resignation:** After losing the 2011 general election to Thaksin’s sister, Yingluck Shinawatra, Abhisit served as Leader of the Opposition. In 2019, following poor election results and his refusal to support the military-led government of Prayut Chan-o-cha, he resigned as Democrat Party leader and later stepped down from Parliament.

---

### 3. Main Challenges Facing His Coalition Government (2008–2011)

Abhisit’s tenure as Prime Minister was fraught with turmoil, marked by deep societal divisions, economic stress, and street violence.

#### A. The Legitimacy Crisis
Abhisit’s government faced an immediate crisis of legitimacy. Supporters of Thaksin Shinawatra (known as the **"Red Shirts"**) viewed Abhisit’s administration as an "accidental government" brought to power by a judicial coup and military backroom deals rather than the ballot box. This fundamental divide destabilized his entire term.

#### B. Mass Protests and Civil Unrest (2009–2010)
* **2009 ASEAN Summit Disruption:** In April 2009, Red Shirt protesters stormed the venue of the ASEAN summit in Pattaya, forcing the embarrassing evacuation of Asian leaders by helicopter and forcing Abhisit to declare a state of emergency.
* **2010 Crackdown:** The crisis peaked between March and May 2010, when tens of thousands of Red Shirts occupied central Bangkok demanding new elections. Abhisit’s government deployed the military to clear the encampments. The resulting violence left over **90 people dead and more than 2,000 injured**, mostly civilians. This event deeply tarnished Abhisit’s international reputation as a democrat and led to legal battles over his responsibility for the deaths (though murder charges against him were later dismissed by Thai courts on jurisdictional grounds).

#### C. Economic Recovery (Global Financial Crisis)
Abhisit took office at the height of the **2008 Global Financial Crisis**. Thailand's export-reliant economy suffered a severe contraction. His government had to launch a massive $42 billion economic stimulus package (*Thai Khem Khaeng*) to fund infrastructure, healthcare, and rural subsidies, attempting to stabilize the economy while competing with Thaksin’s enduring popular appeal in rural areas.

#### D. Fragile Coalition Politics
To keep his government alive, Abhisit relied on a patchwork coalition of smaller parties and opportunistic factions (most notably led by regional kingmaker Newin Chidchob). This made his government vulnerable to internal bargaining, corruption allegations within cabinet ministries, and constant threats of coalition breakdown.

#### E. Border Conflict with Cambodia
His administration faced rising nationalist tensions with Cambodia over disputed territory surrounding the ancient **Preah Vihear Temple**. Skirmishes between Thai and Cambodian troops occurred intermittently between 2008 and 2011, resulting in military and civilian casualties and putting further strain on regional diplomacy.

---

### Summary
Abhisit Vejjajiva was seen by his supporters as an intelligent, corrupt-free, and principled leader capable of restoring institutional stability to Thailand. However, critics view his premiership as a product of establishment intervention that deepened Thailand’s political divide, ultimately defined by the tragic violence of the 2010 political crackdown.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a news report on the political instability in Thailand in 2008 leading up to Abhisit Vejjajiva taking office.
counterfactuals.output:
**SPECIAL REPORT: THAILAND IN CRISIS**

### From Airport Sieges to Judicial Coups: How a Year of Chaos Led to Abhisit’s Rise in Thailand

**BANGKOK** — In December 2008, after a year of unprecedented political turmoil that crippled Thailand’s economy and deeply fractured its society, Oxford-educated Democrat Party leader Abhisit Vejjajiva was named the country’s 27th Prime Minister. 

Abhisit’s rise to power marked the end of a dramatic 12-month political saga characterized by mass street protests, the occupation of government offices, the shutdown of international airports, and controversial court rulings that repeatedly reshuffled the nation's leadership.

---

### A Country Divided: The Pre-Crisis Context

The roots of the 2008 crisis lay in the 2006 military coup that ousted former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra, a populist billionaire whose policies enraged Bangkok’s royalist, military, and urban middle-class establishment while cementing his idol status among the rural poor.

When democratic elections were restored in late 2007, the People’s Power Party (PPP)—a proxy for Thaksin’s loyalists—won a decisive victory. Samak Sundaravej, a fiery right-wing veteran, assumed the premiership in January 2008. However, anti-Thaksin forces refused to accept the outcome, viewing the government as a corrupt puppet regime.

---

### The Yellow Shirts Rise: Occupying the Seat of Power

By May 2008, the People’s Alliance for Democracy (PAD)—popularly known as the "Yellow Shirts" for their allegiance to the Thai monarchy—launched a relentless campaign of civil disobedience. 

Led by media mogul Sondhi Limthongkul, thousands of Yellow Shirts swarmed the streets of Bangkok. The crisis escalated dramatically in August when protesters stormed and occupied Government House, the official workplace of the Prime Minister. For months, Samak’s government was effectively locked out of its own offices, forced to operate from an abandoned airport terminal.

Violence reached a boiling point on October 7, when police used tear gas to disperse protesters besieging Parliament, resulting in two deaths and hundreds of injuries.

---

### Judicial Interventions and Political Shuffles

As street battles intensified, Thailand’s judiciary played a decisive role in stripping pro-Thaksin leaders of power. 

In September, the Constitutional Court forced Prime Minister Samak Sundaravej from office over a technicality—his acceptance of a small payment to host a commercial TV cooking show while in office. 

Somchai Wongsawat, Thaksin’s brother-in-law, succeeded Samak. Rather than appeasing the opposition, Somchai’s appointment enraged the Yellow Shirts, who viewed his leadership as a direct attempt by Thaksin to rule by proxy from self-imposed exile.

---

### The Climax: The Siege of Bangkok’s Airports

In late November, the PAD delivered its most crippling blow to the nation. Seeking to force Somchai’s resignation, thousands of armed and helmeted Yellow Shirts seized control of Suvarnabhumi Airport and Don Mueang Airport, shutting down all commercial flights into and out of Bangkok.

The eight-day blockade paralyzed the country. Over 300,000 foreign tourists were stranded, global supply chains were disrupted, and Thailand’s vital tourism industry suffered billions of dollars in losses. The military refused government orders to clear the airports by force, highlighting a growing rift between the elected government and top commanders.

---

### The Fall of the PPP and the Rise of Abhisit

The stalemate was broken on December 2, 2008, when the Constitutional Court issued a landmark ruling dissolving the ruling PPP and two coalition partners for campaign fraud during the 2007 elections. Somchai Wongsawat was banned from politics for five years and forced to step down immediately.

With the ruling party dissolved, intense behind-the-scenes negotiations took place. Key military figures, led by Army Chief General Anupong Paochinda, reportedly pressured major political factions—most notably the "Friends of Newin" faction led by powerful politician Newin Chidchob—to break away from Thaksin’s network and form a coalition with the opposition Democrat Party.

On December 15, 2008, Thailand’s Parliament held a vote to elect a new leader. Abhisit Vejjajiva won 235 votes against 198 for his rival, officially securing the premiership at the age of 44.

---

### An Uncertain Future

In his inaugural address, Abhisit promised to restore national unity, revitalize the battered economy, and uphold the constitutional monarchy. 

However, political analysts caution that Abhisit’s government faces immense legitimacy challenges. Pro-Thaksin supporters—now organizing as the United Front for Democracy Against Dictatorship (UDD), or "Red Shirts"—have branded Abhisit’s rise a "judicial coup" orchestrated by the military and judicial establishment.

While the immediate chaos of 2008 has subsided with the clearing of the airports and Government House, the deep sociopolitical fault lines that brought Thailand to a standstill remain as fragile as ever.

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain the rapid turnover of Thai prime ministers between 2006 and 2008. Focus on Abhisit Vejjajiva's election by parliament, detailing his credentials, criticisms of his route to power, and quotes from his party's spokesperson regarding national reconciliation.
counterfactuals.output:
Between 2006 and 2008, Thailand experienced profound political volatility, characterized by a rapid succession of prime ministers, street protests, military intervention, and judicial rulings. This turmoil culminated in December 2008 with the parliamentary election of Abhisit Vejjajiva as Prime Minister—a move that temporarily resolved a parliamentary deadlock but further deepened the country's social and political divisions.

---

### 1. Context: The Rapid Turnover of Prime Ministers (2006–2008)

The instability began with the **September 2006 military coup** that ousted the populist Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra. Over the next two years, Thailand was led by five different prime ministers or acting leaders as traditional royalist-military elites battled Thaksin’s rural and working-class supporters:

1. **Surayud Chulanont (Sept 2006 – Jan 2008):** A former army commander installed as interim PM by the military junta following the 2006 coup. 
2. **Samak Sundaravej (Jan 2008 – Sept 2008):** Elected after the pro-Thaksin People’s Power Party (PPP) won the December 2007 general election. He was forced out of office by the Constitutional Court over a bizarre conflict-of-interest ruling regarding his paid appearances on a TV cooking show, amidst massive anti-government protests by the royalist "Yellow Shirts" (People's Alliance for Democracy - PAD).
3. **Somchai Wongsawat (Sept 2008 – Dec 2008):** Thaksin’s brother-in-law, whose brief tenure was crippled by the Yellow Shirts, who seized Bangkok's Government House and blocked the city's main international airports. In December 2008, the Constitutional Court dissolved the PPP for electoral fraud, banning Somchai from politics and forcing his resignation.
4. **Chavarat Charnvirakul (Dec 2008):** Served briefly as acting Prime Minister for less than two weeks while Parliament scrambled to form a new government.

---

### 2. Abhisit Vejjajiva’s Election by Parliament

Following the court-ordered dissolution of the ruling PPP in December 2008, the government dissolved, but Parliament remained intact. Rather than calling a fresh general election, the opposition **Democrat Party**, led by Abhisit Vejjajiva, managed to cobble together a new ruling coalition.

Key to this maneuver was a realignment of factions previously allied with Thaksin—most notably the "Friends of Newin" faction led by Newin Chidchob—which defected to join the Democrats. On **December 15, 2008**, Parliament voted 235 to 198 to elect Abhisit as Thailand’s 27th Prime Minister.

---

### 3. Abhisit Vejjajiva’s Credentials

Abhisit was viewed by Thailand's urban middle class, royalist establishment, and Western diplomats as a polished, technocratic, and reform-minded leader. His credentials included:

* **Elite Education:** Born in the UK to a prominent Anglo-Thai family of medical academics, Abhisit was educated at Eton College and Oxford University, where he earned a bachelor's degree in Philosophy, Politics, and Economics (PPE) and a master's in Economics.
* **Early Political Ascent:** He returned to Thailand, taught economics at Thammasat and Chulachomklao Royal Military Academy, and became one of Thailand’s youngest MPs in 1992 at age 27.
* **Party Leadership:** Known for his eloquent parliamentary debates and clean image, he rose through the Democrat Party ranks to become its leader in 2005. 
* **Public Image:** Abhisit was seen as a smooth-talking, articulate leader capable of appealing to international audiences and restoring institutional integrity to Thai governance after years of perceived corruption under Thaksin.

---

### 4. Criticisms of Abhisit’s Route to Power

Despite his personal credentials, Abhisit’s ascension was deeply controversial and fiercely criticized by pro-Thaksin "Red Shirts" (the United Front for Democracy Against Dictatorship - UDD):

* **"Backroom" Military Intervention:** Critics argued that Abhisit’s coalition was brokered not through democratic mandates, but inside army headquarters. Top military officers, including Army Chief General Anupong Paochinda, allegedly pressured rival MPs and defectors to abandon the pro-Thaksin camp and back Abhisit—a dynamic critics labeled a "silent coup."
* **Lack of a Popular Mandate:** Abhisit’s Democrat Party had not won a general election since 1992. Critics pointed out that he became Prime Minister through parliamentary maneuvering and judicial intervention rather than a direct popular vote.
* **Perceived Judicial Bias:** Pro-Thaksin factions accused the Constitutional Court of a "judicial coup" for dissolving the PPP, arguing that the judiciary acted in tandem with the military and the Democrat Party to strip the majority party of its rightful victory.

---

### 5. Party Spokesperson Quotes and the Push for "National Reconciliation"

Recognizing the crisis of legitimacy surrounding Abhisit’s appointment, the Democrat Party framed his rise as an urgent, constitutionally sound necessity to pull Thailand back from the brink of civil conflict and economic collapse following the airport shutdowns.

**Buranaj Smutharaks**, the official spokesperson for the Democrat Party during this critical transition, repeatedly defended the legitimacy of Abhisit’s government and emphasized the theme of national healing:

* **On the Democratic Process:** Buranaj maintained that Abhisit’s rise complied fully with the constitution, stating that the government was formed to *"restore confidence, pull the country out of economic crisis, and achieve national reconciliation."*
* **On Overcoming Polarization:** Buranaj framed Abhisit’s leadership as a peaceful way forward, noting that the new administration aimed to *"bring back normal democracy to Thailand without resorting to violence or extra-constitutional means."*
* **On Rebuilding Institutional Trust:** Addressing the political divide, Buranaj argued that the Democrat Party was offering an olive branch, stating: *"We extend our invitation to all factions to work together to heal the nation's wounds and re-establish the rule of law."*

### Conclusion

Abhisit’s election in December 2008 brought an end to the rapid turnover of prime ministers that defined 2006–2008, but it did not resolve Thailand's fundamental political crisis. While his supporters viewed him as an educated, principled leader restoring order, his opponents viewed his government as illegitimate. This polarization culminated in massive, bloody Red Shirt protests in Bangkok in 2009 and 2010, proving that parliamentary reconciliation alone could not bridge Thailand's deep political divide.
